newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Dollar seeks foothold after Asian plunge.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Dollar seeks foothold after Asian plunge.

text.p: The dollar struggled to gain a foothold on Monday after tumbling about six yen since Friday as Japanese efforts to talk down the U.S. currency proved more successful than perhaps intended.

On stocks, the London market was dominated by a proposed merger of Grand Metropolitan Plc and Guinness Plc, worth more than 20 billion pounds ($33 billion), to create the world's seventh biggest food and drinks group.

But the Paris market, where drinks and luxury goods company LVMH owns 14 percent of Guinness, seemed to benefit more than London, where the FTSE 100 has risen on 17 of the past 18 trading days. London was moderately lower while Paris was up 0.8 percent.
On the foreign exchange markets, the dollar recovered to 118.42 yen in European trading after sliding to 117.50 yen, its lowest since January, in Tokyo.
"It'll just try to steady today, although there is the risk that we'll get another round of selling," said Lee Ferridge, currency strategist at Commerzbank in London.

U.S. and Japanese interest rates have been the driving force behind the dollar's surge. But late last week U.S. Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan made comments interpreted by markets as a hint that he was now less inclined to raise rates to counter possible inflation.
The Federal Open Market Committee, the central bank's policy-making arm, is due to consider rates on May 20.

The latest dollar slide was triggered by Eisuke Sakakibara, head of the Japanese Finance Ministry's international finance bureau, who said on Saturday the dollar's drop since Friday was "not overly excessive".
A weaker yen helps hard-pressed Japanese exporters but also increases friction with Washington over the Japanese trade surplus.
Japanese officials, who wanted the dollar's surge against the yen to level out, probably got more than they bargained for as the U.S. currency slid.
A senior official of the ruling Liberal Democratic Party then said a dollar/yen rate of around 120 would be the most appropriate level, and that he did not see the yen weakening for some time.
Taku Yamasaki, head of the LDP's policy research council, also said that changing Japan's record-low interest rates would undermine the economy.

"The Japanese officials are worried, they didn't want the dollar to suddenly collapse like this," said Commerzbank's Ferridge. "All they wanted to do was stop the uptrend. They didn't want it to come back down as there's no benefit in Japan seeing a weaker dollar at the moment."
After Yamasaki spoke, the dollar recovered to 118.42 yen by mid morning in Europe but was still below the 120.08 seen in European trade late on Friday.
Japan has kept its interest rates at rock-bottom levels since September 1995, when it slashed its official discount rate to 0.5 percent to keep its economic recovery on track.
Speculation has emerged that the Bank of Japan may tighten its hyper-easy credit given signs the economic recovery is gaining momentum.
But doubts remain whether it will do so quickly, given economic uncertainties and worries over the burden of problem loans at many Japanese banks.
Analysts said expectations of a U.S. rate hike might not revive enough to help the dollar unless U.S. statistics due this week were considerably stronger than expected.
The dollar was also shaky against the mark, standing at 1.6856 marks compared with 1.6843 late on Friday.
On stocks London blue chips sank despite news of the Grand Met and Guinness merger. The FTSE was down 7.1 points at 4,623.8 at midmorning.
After rising 175 points last week, and 379 points or nine percent since April 15, the FTSE was likely to consolidate in the near-term before falling back towards the 4,500 level, one trader said.

Intially the FTSE was up but traders saw the market falling. "The merger has really kept the market afloat this morning but I don't think it will be enough to stop people taking some profits later today," the head of trading at an investment bank said.
But shares in the companies involved leapt. Guinness was up 66-1/2 pence to 583 and Grand Met gained 65 to 580.

In Paris LVMH also jumped 2.32 percent to 1,410 francs. Traders said LVMH would benefit from a reevaluation of its stake in Guinness and the merger with Grand Met could open up new outlets for LVMH brands.
The merger raised spirits throughout the Paris market with the CAC-40 index rising 21.02 points to 2,654.93.

The market was also buoyed by opinion polls which seemed to reassure investors that the ruling centre-right parties were holding their lead over the Socialists for elections at the end of this month and in June.

The German market was weaker, with the DAX index down 11.4 points or 0.32 percent at 3,551.01. Traders said the market was catching up with falls registered on Friday afternoon in electronic trading after the floor had closed.
But Deutsche Telekom was up 1.63 marks at 41.58 on generally positive sentiment before its annual news conference on Tuesday.
STOCK PRICES AT 0900 GMT
London's FTSE 100 was down 7.1 points at 4,623.8.
The Paris CAC-40 index was up 21.02 points (0.8 percent) to 2,654.93.
Frankfurt's DAX index was down 11.40 points at 3,551.01.
CURRENCIES AT 0900 GMT
The dollar stood at 1.6856 marks compared with 1.6843 late in Europe on Friday and 118.42 yen versus 120.08.
PRECIOUS METALS
Gold was at $348.35 after closing at $346.20 an ounce in London on Friday. Silver was up one cent at $4.88. ($ = 0.615 British Pounds)
